p.x:
When I was twelve, my father took me to the bank to open my first account. I was very excited. For years, I had kept all my coins in a big glass jar in my bedroom. That morning, we counted them together: 3,450 baht!
The woman at the bank was very kind. She explained that if I kept my savings in the bank, they would be safe, and I could get money from any ATM with my new card. She said there was no fee for students. She also gave me a small purse with the bank's name on it.
My father gave me some advice that day. "Never borrow money if you can't pay it back," he said. "And be careful when you lend money to friends. Some people forget that they owe you!" He also told me that being rich isn't about how much money you have, but how carefully you spend it. I still remember that.

Getting a loan has never been easier. With a few taps on your phone, you can borrow money in minutes. But before you do, make sure you understand the true cost.
First, look at the interest. A small loan with a high interest rate can grow quickly if you only make the minimum payments. A credit card can be especially dangerous: many charge more than 15% a year. Second, compare the monthly payments with your income. Financial advisers suggest that loan payments should not be more than one third of what you earn.
It also helps to keep a record of every expense. Many banking apps now show your balance in real time and let you transfer money or withdraw cash without visiting a branch. Never share your PIN with anyone, even someone who says they work for the bank. Finally, think about the future. Do you have insurance if you get sick and can't work? Have you included tax in your calculations? If you have money left over at the end of the month, it may be better to invest it than to spend it.

Inflation is sometimes called "the silent thief" because it slowly reduces the value of money without anyone noticing. If prices rise by 3% a year, 100 baht today will buy only around 74 baht's worth of goods in ten years. For people who keep their wealth in cash or low-interest accounts, this can be a serious problem.
Inflation affects some groups more than others. Retired people living on a fixed pension may find it increasingly hard to pay for food and medicine. Young people who rely on an overdraft or credit card debt may find borrowing costs rising as banks increase interest rates. Changes in the exchange rate can make imported goods, such as petrol, even more expensive.
In times of financial uncertainty, scams and fraud also tend to increase. Criminals promise quick ways to make a fortune and target people who are worried about their savings. Experts advise checking every bank statement carefully and being suspicious of any investment that sounds too good to be true. In extreme cases, people who borrow heavily to chase high returns end up bankrupt.
